techniques.name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
techniques.description: MLflow Tracking is the part of the open-source MLflow platform that records each run of a machine learning training script. Developers add logging calls to their code, or switch on automatic logging for supported libraries. Each run's record holds its parameters (the settings chosen, including hyperparameters, which are fixed before training), its metrics (results such as accuracy), the code version, its start and end times, and output files called artefacts, such as the trained model. Runs are grouped into experiments that can be searched and compared in a web interface, and they stay on the developer's machine unless a shared tracking server is set up. The result is a dated record of how each model was built, which a reviewer can use to see what was tried and which run produced the deployed model, but only for what was actually logged.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group develops a diagnostic imaging model across three sites. Ahead of an external assessment, the team exports the logged runs, with the parameters, evaluation metrics, code version and time of each run, so the assessor can see every configuration tried and trace the submitted model to the run that produced it.

A bank's fraud-detection team sees alert precision fall after a retraining. They compare the logged runs for the old and new model, covering parameters, training-dataset reference, code version and metrics, find that a feature setting changed, and note the cause on the run before the next release.

An energy company's data science team keeps every hyperparameter search for its demand-forecasting models on a shared tracking server. When an internal auditor asks why one configuration went live, the team shows the full set of runs searched, their metrics and when each was logged, and the run chosen for deployment.

limitations.description: The record holds only what developers log, plus the default set that automatic logging picks up for supported libraries. A preprocessing choice made in a notebook and never logged is absent, and the log gives no sign that anything is missing, so the audit trail is only as complete as the team's logging habits.

Dataset tracking stores metadata about a dataset, such as its name, a hash of its contents and where it came from, not the data itself. A logged run can show which dataset was used but cannot restore it, so reproducing a result needs the data to be versioned or retained separately.

A tracking server is a working store, not a sealed ledger. Runs can be marked as deleted and tags overwritten by anyone with write access, so the log supports an audit only if access is restricted and the store is backed up.

Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively. Where that is not done, the record of one stage will not show what fed it.

Artefact storage grows with every logged model and file, so heavy experimentation with large models raises storage costs. Deleting old runs to save space removes part of the record that an audit would rely on.

resources.title: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow
resources.abstract: Machine learning development creates multiple new challenges that are not present in a traditional software development lifecycle. These include keeping track of the myriad inputs to an ML application (e.g., data versions, code and tuning parameters), reproducing results, and production deployment. In this paper, we summarize these challenges from our experience with Databricks customers, and describe MLflow, an open source platform we recently launched to streamline the machine learning lifecycle. MLflow covers three key challenges: experimentation, reproducibility, and model deployment, using generic APIs that work with any ML library, algorithm and programming language. The project has a rapidly growing open source community, with over 50 contributors since its launch in June 2018.

resources.title: MLflow Tracking Quickstart
An MLOps Framework for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection with MLflow
resources.abstract: The surge in network traffic has required advanced techniques to ensure network security. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs), which increasingly employ Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methodologies, play a pivotal role in this task by continuously monitoring network traffic patterns and identifying suspicious activities. To address the complexities of developing ML- and DL-based NIDS, MLOps tools have been designed to optimize model deployment, monitoring, and management in production environments, streamlining model development. These tools enable efficient experimentation, version management, and logging of artifacts for network administrators and data scientists. In this work, we design a framework powered by MLflow to manage the ML pipeline from data handling to results visualization. To show the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted an experimental campaign on 4 broadly used security datasets (viz. NSL-KDD, IoT-23, Kitsune, and TON_IoT) performing crucial tasks for intrusion detection, namely anomaly detection, binary misuse detection, and multiclass misuse detection.

resources.title: Enhancing Quantum Software Development Process with Experiment Tracking
resources.abstract: As quantum computing advances from theoretical promise to experimental reality, the need for rigorous experiment tracking becomes critical. Drawing inspiration from best practices in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), we argue that reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in quantum research can benefit significantly from structured tracking workflows. This paper explores the application of MLflow in quantum research, illustrating how it enables better development practices, experiment reproducibility, decision making, and cross-domain integration in an increasingly hybrid classical-quantum landscape.

The deployed fraud-detection model can be traced to the logged run that produced it, including that run's parameters, code version and evaluation metrics

Changes in parameters, code version and evaluation metrics between successive releases of the clinical risk model are recorded in the tracking log and available to the clinical safety team before each release
The development log for the demand-forecasting model is held on an access-controlled, backed-up tracking server, and no run has been deleted since the model was approved

techniques.name: Data Version Control
techniques.description: Data Version Control (DVC) is an open-source tool that records which version of a dataset or model was used at each point in a machine learning project. It works alongside Git, the standard system for tracking changes to code. DVC keeps large data and model files in separate storage, such as a cloud storage service, and puts a small pointer file into Git that holds a fingerprint (hash) of the file's contents. A team can also describe a pipeline, meaning the ordered steps from raw data through preprocessing to a trained model, and DVC then records fingerprints of each step's inputs, settings and outputs. Committed to Git, these files give a dated history of how data and models changed and let the team restore an earlier version, but only for what was added to DVC and committed.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a chest X-ray classifier. When a regulator asks which images and preprocessing produced the version it submitted, the group checks out the tagged Git commit, shows the dataset fingerprints and pipeline steps recorded in it, and restores that exact data to confirm.

A lender's credit-scoring team sees approval rates shift after a quarterly data refresh. Using DVC with Git, they list the files that changed between the datasets behind the last two model releases, trace the shift to one refresh, and decide whether to revert to the earlier data version.

A flood-forecasting agency versions its river-sensor calibration data and the feature-extraction steps that use it. When a forecast is challenged, an independent reviewer can see from the version history who changed the calibration data and when, and which model release was trained on each version.

A manufacturer's quality team retrains a defect-detection model each month and tags each release in Git with the DVC record of its training images. When a customer reports a missed defect, the team retrieves the exact images behind the model then in use and sees what was added or removed since the previous release.

limitations.description: DVC records only what has been added to it and committed to Git. Data edited outside DVC, or changes that were never committed, leave no trace, and nothing in the history shows what is missing, so the record is only as complete as the team's habits.

Lineage exists only for steps defined as DVC pipeline stages. A study of 56 open-source projects found that 85.7% used only DVC's versioning and tracking feature, so a project that uses DVC may hold no record of how its data was preprocessed or its model trained.

Restoring an earlier model takes more than DVC's files. The code, the software environment and the stored data must all still exist, and the pipeline lock file records commands, file fingerprints and parameter values but not library versions, so a restored pipeline can still give different results.

Scale costs time and storage. A changed data file is stored again as a new copy, and the documentation notes that operations such as pulling become slow with tens of thousands of files, pointing teams that need to branch and merge large datasets in object storage to a different tool.
When several people change the same data files or pipeline, merge conflicts in DVC's tracking files have to be resolved by hand. Without agreed branching rules the history becomes hard to trust.

resources.title: Get Started with DVC
On the Co-evolution of ML Pipelines and Source Code - Empirical Study of DVC Projects
resources.abstract: The growing popularity of machine learning (ML) applications has led to the introduction of software engineering tools such as Data Versioning Control (DVC), MLFlow and Pachyderm that enable versioning ML data, models, pipelines and model evaluation metrics. Since these versioned ML artifacts need to be synchronized not only with each other, but also with the source and test code of the software applications into which the models are integrated, prior findings on co-evolution and coupling between software artifacts might need to be revisited. Hence, in order to understand the degree of coupling between ML-related and other software artifacts, as well as the adoption of ML versioning features, this paper empirically studies the usage of DVC in 391 Github projects, 25 of which in detail. Our results show that more than half of the DVC files in a project are changed at least once every one-tenth of the project's lifetime. Furthermore, we observe a tight coupling between DVC files and other artifacts, with 1/4 pull requests changing source code and 1/2 pull requests changing tests requiring a change to DVC files. As additional evidence of the observed complexity associated with adopting ML-related software engineering tools like DVC, an average of 78% of the studied projects showed a non-constant trend in pipeline complexity.

resources.title: DVC in Open Source ML-development: The Action and the Reaction
resources.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems are gaining popularity, reshaping various domains ranging from customer services to software engineering. The effectiveness of ML systems is dependent on the quality of their training data. Therefore, practitioners invest substantial time experimenting with different data, parameters, and models to guarantee the quality of the end system. Prior work highlighted unique challenges of developing ML systems, particularly concerning versioning data and models. Recently, various tools such as DVC and MLFlow have emerged to aid developers in the storage and tracking of data. Despite their growing popularity, very little is known about their usage patterns and impact on open-source software (OSS) systems. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study on 56 GitHub OSS projects that use DVC to understand the DVC usage pattern and the impact of using DVC on the software development process. We found that Versioning and tracking is the most adopted DVC feature, being utilized by all 56 projects and being the only adopted feature in 85.7% of them. Furthermore, we found that DVC has a significant impact on the software development process indicators such as the number of created pull requests (PRs), and the number of bug-fix commits. For instance, our findings showed that DVC causes a peak in the number of commits and PRs at the moment of the adoption, followed by a long-term decrease. We believe that our findings can assist practitioners in tailoring tools to better meet user requirements and help organizations realize potential outcomes of adopting such tools.

techniques.name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
techniques.description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

example_use_cases.description: A fraud-scoring API provider examines each client's query stream for runs of near-identical transactions altered in small steps, which suggest someone is probing for the score at which a transaction passes. Flagged accounts are rate-limited and sent to the security team for review.

A company selling traffic-sign recognition as a paid API tests whether the spacing between each customer's successive image queries follows the pattern ordinary use produces. Accounts whose queries look synthetic and widely spread, as in model-copying attacks, are flagged for investigation and possible suspension.

A health-technology company serving a paediatric triage model to many clinics monitors each clinic's query volumes and the ages in its requests. A clinic sending mostly adult patients, or a sudden change after a software update, is flagged so the company can contact it before unsafe advice is given.

A provider of a text-generation API scores each customer's usage by how often prompts and responses are flagged as harmful and whether jailbreak attempts recur. Customers with high scores go to review, which can lead to a warning or suspension.

A bank's model risk team compares the monthly log of calls to its credit-scoring API, by internal team and purpose, with the uses approved at validation. The comparison is filed in the model's audit record, so reviewers can see whether the model is used as documented.

limitations.description: Anomalies are defined against a baseline of normal use, and ordinary users can be unusual. In PRADA's tests, legitimate queries made of consecutive frames from a sequence triggered false alarms at stricter settings, so the alert threshold has to be tuned to each model and use case.

A patient attacker can stay inside normal limits by querying slowly, adding dummy queries or spreading queries across many accounts. PRADA's authors show that padding queries raises the attacker's cost three to ten times, and that multiple accounts defeat per-account analysis.

Useful monitoring needs request content, or features of it, to be logged and sometimes read by reviewers. For sensitive applications that may be unlawful or unacceptable, and Microsoft notes that detection may be less accurate when human review is switched off for such customers.

Detectors keep state for every account. PRADA's authors estimate a few gigabytes in total for a few hundred clients of an image model, and the cost rises with traffic and with the retention period set for audit evidence.

The published extraction detectors were tested on small models, decision trees in one case and image classifiers in the other, against simulated attackers. Kesarwani et al. describe their warning as approximate, so an alert is a lead for investigation, not proof of theft.

resources.title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
resources.abstract: Machine learning models deployed on the cloud are susceptible to several security threats including extraction attacks. Adversaries may abuse a model's prediction API to steal the model thus compromising model confidentiality, privacy of training data, and revenue from future query payments. This work introduces a model extraction monitor that quantifies the extraction status of models by continually observing the API query and response streams of users. We present two novel strategies that measure either the information gain or the coverage of the feature space spanned by user queries to estimate the learning rate of individual and colluding adversaries. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them against state of the art extraction attacks. We demonstrate empirical performance results of these approaches for decision tree and neural network models using open source datasets and BigML MLaaS platform.

resources.title: PRADA: Protecting Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) applications are increasingly prevalent. Protecting the confidentiality of ML models becomes paramount for two reasons: (a) a model can be a business advantage to its owner, and (b) an adversary may use a stolen model to find transferable adversarial examples that can evade classification by the original model. Access to the model can be restricted to be only via well-defined prediction APIs. Nevertheless, prediction APIs still provide enough information to allow an adversary to mount model extraction attacks by sending repeated queries via the prediction API. In this paper, we describe new model extraction attacks using novel approaches for generating synthetic queries, and optimizing training hyperparameters. Our attacks outperform state-of-the-art model extraction in terms of transferability of both targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples (up to +29-44 percentage points, pp), and prediction accuracy (up to +46 pp) on two datasets. We provide take-aways on how to perform effective model extraction attacks. We then propose PRADA, the first step towards generic and effective detection of DNN model extraction attacks. It analyzes the distribution of consecutive API queries and raises an alarm when this distribution deviates from benign behavior. We show that PRADA can detect all prior model extraction attacks with no false positives.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: C2PA Content Credentials
techniques.description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

example_use_cases.description: An image-generation service offered in the EU attaches a signed manifest to every image it returns, declaring an AI 'created' action with the service as signer, as its means of meeting the AI Act's Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format. Its compliance team validates a weekly sample of outputs to decide whether marking is working, and registers a watermark soft binding so that a stripped image can be matched back to its record.

A news agency's verification desk runs every image sent in by the public through a C2PA validator before publication. A trusted manifest recording capture on a named camera, with no AI-generated ingredients, lets editors publish it with a provenance label. A manifest naming a generative tool, or a hash that no longer matches, sends it to forensic review, and an image with no credentials is treated as of unknown origin, not as authentic.

An insurer's claims app lets assessors apply an AI tool that enhances and annotates photographs of vehicle damage, and records each AI edit as an action in the photograph's manifest. When a claim is disputed, a reviewing assessor or the claimant's representative can see which changes the AI tool made and check them against the retained original, which the edited photograph's manifest cites as an ingredient.

A social-media platform reads Content Credentials on upload, labels images whose trusted manifest declares a generative AI source, and shows users who signed the record. Its trust-and-safety team tracks what share of uploads carry trusted, untrusted or no credentials, to decide how far its synthetic-media policy can rely on the labels and where it still needs other detection methods.

limitations.description: The record is easy to lose. Anyone can remove the manifest, an attack the C2PA's own threat model expects, and the file is then an ordinary file with no link to its history unless a watermark or fingerprint soft binding was registered with a manifest repository. Because credentials are optional and removable, a file without them says nothing about its origin: the absence of a manifest cannot show that content is human-made or unaltered.

A valid manifest shows who signed the record and that what its hash covers is unchanged, not that its statements are true. A signer can omit an AI step, a stolen key yields manifests that validate, and a camera photographing a screen signs a genuine capture of a staged scene. Validators need not check revocation, metadata such as location may sit outside the hash, and a 2026 preprint found validators disagreeing on the same file, so a result depends on the signer, validator and trust list.

The history is complete only while every tool in the workflow supports C2PA. An edit made in an unsupported tool is not recorded, and if the file later passes through a supporting tool, the new signer implicitly vouches for that unrecorded change, so the chain can show fewer steps than took place. The C2PA itself says the approach depends on widespread adoption by tools and platforms.

Manifests can disclose more than the creator intends, such as capture time and place, device details, the edit history and, through the separate Creator Assertions Working Group identity extension, who made the content. The C2PA's threat model lists identifying creators and tracking viewers as risks. Assertions can be redacted when a file is reused as an ingredient, but people working in risky settings, such as human-rights documentation, must decide what to include before signing.

Support for AI-generated text is immature. Embedding a manifest in plain text, as invisible Unicode characters, entered the specification in version 2.3 and is still marked as under review; the reference SDK supports it only behind an unstable option, and any edit to the text breaks the hash. For language-model output the method is much less dependable than for images, video and audio, where embedding is established.

techniques.name: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Model Inference
techniques.description: A zero-knowledge proof of model inference lets the owner of a model show an outside party that one specific model, fixed in advance, turns a particular input into a particular output, without revealing the model's weights. The owner publishes a commitment to the weights, a short cryptographic fingerprint such as a hash that binds them without disclosing them, together with a verification key that fixes the model's architecture. The model's arithmetic is converted to whole numbers (quantised) and written as a system of equations called a circuit, and for each input a proving system produces a proof, of a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes, that this circuit, run with weights matching the commitment, turns that input into that output; the input can be public or committed in the same way. Anyone holding the verification key can check the proof in milliseconds to seconds: it shows that the committed model gives that output for that input, while keeping the weights hidden, and says nothing about whether that model is accurate, fair or safe. Unlike homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on data it cannot read but gives the caller no evidence of which computation was run, and unlike model signing, which lets someone who holds a model's files check who released them, it lets someone who never sees the weights check individual outputs against them.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-scoring vendor publishes the weight commitment in the report of an independent bias and accuracy audit, which was run on the quantised model bound to that commitment. When a refused applicant complains, the lender's complaints team asks the vendor for a proof for that decision and checks it against the published commitment, to confirm that the audited model gives the same refusal on the applicant's data before it reviews the decision itself.

A hospital trust buying chest X-ray triage results from a cloud provider writes into the contract that its clinical engineering team may challenge a random sample of each month's results. For each sampled case the provider must return a proof against the commitment to the model the trust validated, and the team treats a failed or missing proof as evidence that a different model was served, which triggers the contract's audit clause.

An online-safety regulator inspecting the age-estimation service a platform relies on submits its own test images and asks for a proof with each estimate. Its inspectors check each proof against the commitment registered when an accredited laboratory certified the vendor's model, to decide whether the service in use is the certified model, without the vendor handing its proprietary weights to the regulator.

limitations.description: A valid proof shows that the committed weights turn this input into this output. It does not show that the model is accurate, fair or safe, that the input was genuine, or that the service ran the committed model: a different model giving the same output passes too, so spot checks catch a substituted model only on inputs where the two disagree. A commitment carries assurance only if an audit was run on the model it binds.

Proving costs far more than running the model. Published figures: 88 seconds per prediction of a 15-million-parameter VGG16 on CIFAR-10 images (zkCNN), about 41 minutes for an ImageNet-scale MobileNet on a large cloud server (Kang et al.), and about 13 minutes for one 2,048-token pass of a 13-billion-parameter language model on a data-centre GPU, after a one-off 16-minute commitment (zkLLM). Proving every output of a busy service is impractical, so protocols prove sampled or disputed outputs.

The proof covers a quantised, whole-number version of the model, not the floating-point model that was trained and perhaps audited, and the two can give slightly different outputs. Published attacks plant backdoors that stay dormant at full precision and activate only after quantisation, which EZKL's security notes flag. Audits and accuracy tests must therefore be run on the quantised model that is actually proved, or the commitment and the audit describe different models.

The guarantee depends on configuration. If the weights are private inputs with no published commitment, a proof shows only that some weights for the stated architecture give the output. Hashing the weights inside the proof keeps them hidden but costs about as much again as proving the inference. EZKL's cheaper settings, including its Python default, bind the weights without fully hiding them, and its notes warn they can be recovered from enough proofs. The architecture is normally disclosed.

Soundness rests on the software as well as the mathematics. A compiler error that leaves the equations under-constrained can let a false proof verify, a risk EZKL's documentation names, and EZKL's proofs rely on public parameters from a multi-party set-up ceremony. Audits cover specific releases (EZKL's covered version 21), so verifiers should fix which tool versions and parameters they accept. EZKL, the most used tool, has had no open-source licence since January 2024.
